work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In Noe et filios eius, de cherubim et in propthetam Oseam

paragraphs.text: The order of what came before calls our discourse to Noah and to the whole subject of his story, and wishes to give it its proper course in due order. For this is what the discourse promises you, and what your zeal for learning is waiting for. But since the evening hour is short and the ideas are many, I do not want to be ruled by the shortness of the time and leave out the breadth of the ideas. So I will set this subject aside for another discourse, and today let us begin for you with the voice of the prophet.

The blessed Hosea, who is counted among the twelve prophets, calls those who share his way of life to the works of righteousness, and at the very outset he sets before us a parable taken from farming, saying something like this: "Sow for righteousness, and harvest the fruit of life." The end of unrighteousness is death; the end of righteousness is life. "Sow for yourselves for righteousness, and harvest the fruit of life." See how what Adam lost is given back. Back then he was kept from touching the tree of life and was cast out of paradise. He is commanded not to touch the tree so that God might show that he cast the man out not because he hated him but to discipline him. "Harvest the fruit of life" is as if one were saying: that which Adam lost.

"Sow for yourselves for righteousness, and harvest the fruit of life," since everyone who sows scatters to all appearances but in truth gathers. Sowing looks like scattering, but its power and its promise are those of gathering. For the sower scatters not in order to lose but in order to gather more. That is why David likens almsgiving to the poor to sowing, when he says: "He has scattered, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever and ever."

Adam was cast out of paradise. For I want to set out some of the ideas that were passed over, which the grace of the Holy Spirit itself placed in the Scriptures; but I am hemmed in by the sheer number of ideas. Adam was cast out of paradise, or rather he was sent away, and God sets the cherubim around paradise as guards. "For God stationed," it says, "the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way to the tree of life." See how God everywhere presents one appearance and accomplishes something else. He stationed the cherubim in the guise of guards, but in truth as comforters. Why were the cherubim stationed there? Was the flaming sword that turns not enough to stop anyone who tried to get in?

But the account of the cherubim is a strange one. If anyone has read the blessed Ezekiel's account of the cherubim, or rather the vision he saw face to face, he sees in the cherubim themselves the pledge of our life. "For I saw," he says, "the living creatures, the cherubim, by the river Chebar, and the heavens were opened, and I saw the chariot of the cherubim, eight wings to each one; and under the wings of the cherubim there was the face of a lion, the face of an eagle, the face of a calf, the face of a man."

So, since Adam had been cast out of paradise, the very sight of the guard pledged hope to him, so that he would not cut himself off from hope as one who had become an outcast. "Do not cut yourself off from hope," it says. "Do not despair of your salvation. You have not been cast out of paradise. See your own image being guarded in me, and see the divine mystery and God's design." He chose the most royal of the splendid creatures known among men. Among four-footed beasts nothing is more royal than the lion, among birds nothing more royal than the eagle, among farm animals nothing more royal than the ox, and among all creatures nothing more royal than man. The ox drives on the work of farming, the lion that of kingship, the eagle the heights of piety, and man the word of godliness.

The cherubim, brothers, are described in divine Scripture as intelligent and spiritual living beings, full of eyes. To set the sight before you as in a picture: have you seen the markings of the peacock? Have you seen the images of eyes on that bird? What in the peacock is an appearance that has the shape of eyes but not the power of eyes, in the cherubim is a sight attested together with the reality itself. It flashes forth power and offers a truly all-radiant sight for understanding.

And pay attention. In the Hebrew tongue "cherubim" is interpreted as "fullness of knowledge," and in this God is seated. For since God is enthroned in wisdom, and God's throne is nothing other than wisdom, God is described as seated upon the cherubim: "You who are seated upon the cherubim, show yourself." This shows that God's throne and resting place is the many-eyed wisdom that sees all things and has nothing blind in it. It searches all things, both those above and those below; it seeks out the things present and searches out the things to come. It tells of the nature of angels and suggests angelic speech; it inspires prophets and grants discernment to apostles.

And the cherubim were full of knowledge. That is why it says: "And the cherubim were full of eyes, and their backs and their feet were full of eyes." For in wisdom nothing is blind, nothing idle. Our whole body is blind except for the eyes. No one sees with a hand or with the back; the darkened body is lit by a single lamp, the eye. But there the intelligent natures see wholly and throughout: such a being is all eye, all hand, all worker, all seeing wisdom. This is what "seated upon the cherubim" means: it stands for "resting upon the wisdom that [?]." For just as our bodies [need?] rest, so thrones provide rest and honor. A throne is both a symbol of honor and a relief for bodies. We comfort our weary bodies by inviting them to sit on a throne, but he neither suffers nor undergoes toil; he remains, and rests upon wisdom.

So God rests upon every virtue, and divine Scripture also calls this a throne. That is why Scripture does not speak of one throne of God but of many different ones. It called heaven a throne: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet." It spoke of God's throne as established upon the winds. For it says that when he was preparing his own throne, he had a throne of fire upon the winds: "His throne," it says, "is a blazing fire."

Sometimes he is enthroned upon winds, sometimes upon flame, sometimes upon heaven, sometimes in a soul that loves God, so that you may not suppose that the throne of heaven is bodily. Nothing circumscribes God, but all things are circumscribed by God. When Jerusalem's piety was at its height, when it had pure worship and guileless adoration, the Scriptures called it the throne of God. Jeremiah cries out: "And they shall call Jerusalem the throne of the Lord." For he does not have a throne as one bounded by a place; wherever he finds holiness to rest in, there he is enthroned. I know that Paul and Peter are thrones of Christ; I know that every martyr's soul is a throne of God; every soul on which he rests, he calls a throne. That is why, when the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles, it did not simply come upon them, and Scripture did not simply say that it dwelt in them. Rather, "there appeared," it says, "tongues as of fire, and they sat upon each one of them." Do you see them becoming thrones?

So for Adam's sake God stationed the cherubim, bearing the face of the man who had been driven out, so that he might learn that even though cast out he still has a pledge with those who stand guard. And see the marvel. He did not clothe Adam in paradise with as much dignity as the glory with which he later clothed the saints. This was to show that glory is not confined to a place; it is virtue that puts on glory. Adam transgressed in paradise and was cast out, while the saints were crowned outside paradise and so entered into it. A flaming sword drove Adam out; a chariot of fire caught Elijah up. This was to show that it was not the nature of fire that fought against Adam, but his transgression that turned all things into his enemies. Think of Elijah before his ascension, giving orders to fire, the very thing that had been a terror to Adam. The flaming sword frightened Adam, while holy Elijah, though he lived on earth, gave orders to heaven, called down thunderbolts and brought them down upon the ungodly. One could see a man commanding thunderbolts and striking his opponents with fire.

See how disobedience and obedience are set in order. Adam disobeyed, and he trembles before fire; Elijah obeyed, and he gives orders to fire. A flaming sword pursues Adam, and a furnace of fire refreshes the three young men with dew. For this reason God gave the saints prizes greater than life in paradise, so that by sharing in better things they might have the hope of being called back to their original state.

Paradise was shut to Adam, and Peter is entrusted with the keys of heaven. See from what Adam was cast out, and with what Peter is entrusted: "To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven." What did that man lose that could compare with what [this one] found [?]

Did the lowliness of their surroundings keep them from attaining virtue and setting things right? And what am I saying? Adam is in paradise and is condemned for transgression, while Job sits on a dung heap and is crowned for his endurance. Paradise did Adam no good, because his ways did not match his place, and the lowliness of his place did Job no harm, because he was adorned by his ways.

And one could see extraordinary wonders granted to the saints. Look at the goodness of God and the abundance of gifts he has: he granted many things to many people, yet gave each of those he gifted a grace of his own. Great indeed, truly great, is the blessed Elijah, taken up in a chariot of fire. Wonderful are the three young men, who trod upon the flame and carried pledges of immortality in mortal bodies. When I see the furnace giving off dew, I marvel; when I see the lions muzzled, I am astounded. As for the beauty of the miracle concerning Hananiah, neither does this one yield to that, nor that one to this. All of them shine, and not one is overshadowed by another.

And see what God does to show that he honors virtues, not bodies. He paints on our souls the age at which a righteous man practiced his virtue. No one has ever pictured Joseph in his mind as an old man. Your own conscience is witness that the mind always pictures him as young, even though he died at a hundred and ten. But since his virtue did not reach its peak in old age, and instead blossomed in his youth, he is remembered at the age at which he endured his contests. Who, on hearing about Abraham, has ever imagined him as young or pictured him with the features of a young man? Was he not younger once, and a youth? Did he not pass through the whole span of youth? But nothing he did in his youth was recorded. God called him to piety when he was seventy-five years old, and from then on he lived a life of virtue in his old age. So every mind that pictures his features paints him as an old man. Likewise we all picture Isaac as young, since nothing else about him is recorded except the time when the hour of the sacrifice came. God honors with remembrance the age at which the saints did the deeds of virtue. He does not dishonor their other ages; he dignifies those in which virtue shone most beautifully. The three young men went into the furnace and lived many years after their martyrdom, and the hymn of the three young men is heard to this day. Did they not grow older? Did they not grow old? Yet every other age of theirs is passed over in silence, and the one in which they shone is remembered. Adam, however, was formed perfect from the first. He never went through youth, but appeared perfect the moment he came into being, for the first creation could not appear imperfect.

So he was cast out of paradise, to keep to the line we were following before. Yet outside paradise his sons were given greater things than those in paradise, so that the things to come might be greater than those that went before. Listen. Because of his transgression Adam heard, "You are earth, and to earth you shall return": though he lived, he was made subject to death. The apostles, by contrast, raise the dead to life. It is one thing to be kept in life, another to be a fountain of life for others as well.

Paradise was shut to Adam, but for Paul heaven itself was opened along with paradise: "I know a man who fourteen years ago (whether in the body or out of the body I do not know; God knows) was caught up into paradise, and was caught up to the third heaven." See how greater honors were given to the children.

And here is the marvel. Joshua son of Nun bridled not only earthly fire but heavenly fire as well. His voice stopped the sun as it was running and completing its own course, putting his word on it like a bridle. He was about to rout the enemy, but evening was already coming on and would have left his achievement unfinished. So, so that the course of the sun would not stand in the way of completing the victory, he took courage and said: "Let the sun stand still over Gibeon." See the marvel.

Let the heretics be ashamed. The servant gave orders to the sun without praying, yet they reduce the Master of the prophets to the rank of a servant and say that Christ can do nothing without entreating the Father. "Let the sun stand still." And it stood still. The word became a bridle for the great light, so that the pagans might learn the difference between believers and unbelievers: believers give orders to the very things the pagans worship.

God stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way to the tree of life. The prophet led us into this line of thought when he said, "Sow for yourselves for righteousness": what transgression lost, the practice of the virtues has found.

But the story of Hosea is a strange one. This very saying of the prophet is a stumbling block to the ungodly but a support to the faithful. "The beginning of the words of the Lord to Hosea. And the Lord said to the prophet: Go, take for yourself a wife of harlotry and children of harlotry." How many unbelievers has this phrase troubled? How many unbelievers has ignorance led into perplexity? The believer, even if he were minded to blaspheme, would find no grounds for it. "Was it fitting," someone says, "for a holy and venerable mouth to begin a prophecy with a profane word? And God said to the prophet: Go, take a wife of harlotry." The teacher of chastity, the herald of righteousness, the one who hates what is profane, who set before us the pattern of purity, told his own prophet, who served him with piety, to take a wife of harlotry.

Many, not understanding this, have turned the passage into allegory. But it is not allegory; it is a true account of what happened. When you learn the context, you find the solution. As I have often said before, and will not stop saying, the solution to every difficulty is the context of the passage in question.

God is accustomed to liken the word of godliness to a bridegroom who takes a bride, lives with her, and has children by her. For what a husband is to a wife, the word is to the soul: it makes her ready to give birth and to conceive truth. Paul is a witness, when he says: "For I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy, for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." And John the Baptist, bearing witness to the Savior, said: "You yourselves know from the beginning that I said, I am not the Christ, but I have been sent ahead of him. He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend who stands and listens rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. My joy has been made complete. He must increase, but I must decrease." A servant's glory is his master's splendor.

So the New Testament showed the Word in the role of bridegroom, the soul as the one being wedded, and the Word filling her with divine plantings so that she might bear the fruit of righteousness. In the Old Testament, Scripture plainly presents God saying to the synagogue: "Remember the days of your youth, how I brought you out of the land of Egypt, and saw you naked and in shame; and I clothed you with garments, and the hair of your head grew, and you became my wife. And you forsook me, and committed adultery with wood and stone, and forgot me, says the Lord."

Pay attention, I beg you. The Word of God, then, is the husband and bridegroom of the soul, but his union with her is not like bodily marriage. Bodily marriage begins with desire; the soul's wedding begins with fear. There desire is the forerunner of marriage; here fear is the forerunner of this holy union. That is why the prophet Isaiah says: "Because of the fear of you, O Lord, we conceived in the womb, and were in labor, and gave birth to a spirit of salvation."

See the prophet giving birth. The one who says this is a man, so that you may not suspect anything to do with bodily matter: it belongs to a man to beget, not to conceive and give birth. The male takes up words that, as far as the nature of bodies goes, do not suit everyone, but as far as the soul goes suit everyone, man and woman alike, and he says: "Because of the fear of you, O Lord, we conceived in the womb, and were in labor, and gave birth to a spirit of salvation." Paul, being his brother (for he too had a soul wedded to the divine Word), likewise takes up the voice of a woman in labor and says to the Galatians: "My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you."

In the same way, brothers, rain is called the husband of the earth. In the natural order a woman cannot give birth without a man, nor can the earth give birth without rain, and so divine Scripture presents rain as the earth's husband. God says: "Just as, when the rain comes down from heaven, it does not return until it has drenched the earth, and the earth brings forth." For the earth gives birth with rain as its spouse and husband. That is why the apostle Paul says: "For land that drinks the rain that often falls on it, and brings forth vegetation useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated." When you hear of bodies, you think of the experiences proper to bodies; but when you hear of the earth giving birth, you do not imagine desire for marriage or intercourse, and in taking in the childbearing of lifeless earth you read nothing human into it. Think of the bride of the divine Word in just the same way. It is fear that weds the soul, and that is why what is born is a spiritual offspring. "We gave birth," it says, "to a spirit of salvation." And since it is spirit that we conceived, the Lord says in the Gospel: "What is born of the Spirit is spirit."

Now that you know the story, receive the solution to the disputed points. God had the synagogue like a married woman whose husband was the law. She went whoring away from piety and fell into the adultery of idolatry, for what adultery is in a woman, idolatry is in a soul. They drifted off toward many gods; they abandoned the One who is and loved those that are not. Again and again the prophets urged them, and they received promises of good things and threats of evils, yet they did not turn back from wickedness. So God presents the brazenness of the Jews' ingratitude in the figure of a harlot. For he says to the prophet: "Take for yourself a wife of harlotry."

First, then, as to the act being unlawful: God did not want the prophet to commit fornication; he wanted the harlot to be brought to chastity. He did not command him, nor even simply allow him, to unite himself with a harlot. He commanded him to take her out of harlotry and join her to himself as his wife. That is why it says, "Take for yourself a wife of harlotry and children of harlotry": that is, for bearing children, not for satisfying desire, so that she might become fruitful and bring forth fruits worthy of the prophet's teachings.
Why, then, "Take for yourself a wife of harlotry"? "Because," it says, "the land will go utterly whoring." He sets that harlot over against the people's harlotry, their whoring away from God.

"And he went and took Gomer, and he gave a gomer of barley and a nebel of wine." What need was there, or what benefit to the reader or hearer, in learning that the prophet took a harlot, and how he paid her, and how much? It is not for nothing that Scripture brings in the matter of the payment. The gift that persuaded the harlot to be chaste was paltry. Out of regard for a small measure of barley, and shamed by a little measure of wine, she renounced harlotry and pledged herself to honorable marriage. So God orders the amount of the payment to be written down, in order to shame the synagogue, which was the true harlot. The one was shamed by a small measure into putting away harlotry and came to love honorable marriage. But the synagogue was not shamed into renouncing the harlotry of idols and pledging herself to the honor of marriage, neither by regard for the manna, nor by the provision of forty years, nor by the rocks split open to bring forth water, nor by the rod that blossomed, nor by the corpses of the Egyptians, nor by the wonders in the wilderness, nor by the land of promise, nor by the gifts from heaven, nor by the sun reined in, nor by the moon, nor by the whole creation serving her.

That harlot was also a type of the nations, who once worshiped idols and were later called to the honorable marriage of the Gospel. "Go, take for yourself a wife of harlotry and children of harlotry." Do not refuse to do what I do. For I too take the Church that is to be my bride out of harlotry. So imitate what I do. Just as I am not ashamed of her who is to be taken out of harlotry and made holy, so you too must not look at the harlot's former life and despair of her chastity in the future.

"Take for yourself a wife of harlotry"; and he went and took her. Then the harlot conceives and gives birth. When she had given birth, God says to him: "Call her name Not Pitied." Again she gives birth, and God says to him: "Call his name Not My People." Consider the meaning of this. Have you ever seen a baby called by the name Not My People? Yet the Master commanded and the servant obeyed. It was a riddle about the people who were once neither loved nor called a people, but afterward came to knowledge. For much further on, since a great deal comes in between, God says to the prophet: "And it shall be that in the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, they shall be called sons of the living God."

We did not think these things up by ourselves; we have been supplied with them by the words of the apostle: "As it is also written in Hosea the prophet: I will call Not My People my people, and her who was not loved, beloved. And it shall be that in the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, there they shall be called sons of the living God." Moses said this long before: "They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god, and I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation."

“In the place,” he says, “where it was said, ‘Not my people’”: that is, the law that called them “Not a people” will call them “sons of the living God.” See how the apostles reflect one another. Paul says, “As he says also in Hosea: ‘I will call Not-my-people my people.’” And Peter, in the catholic epistles, says to the faithful, “Sanctified brothers, who once were Not-a-people, but now are a people.” And since it is written, “Call her name Not-beloved,” he says, “who once were not beloved, but now have even been shown mercy beyond measure.” This is why the prophetic choir also calls the Church the bride of Christ: she is taken out of harlotry and brought to chaste marriage. Falling away is a corruption of bodies; transgression is a corruption of both body and soul. For this reason the Savior calls the Church his spouse, and Paul does not shrink from saying, “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself up for her,” so that he might sanctify her in both body and spirit.

The heretics paid no attention to “he gave himself up.” Instead, their minds were wounded by reading badly what was written well, and see what clever argument they have devised. They say, “It is written by Paul about the Son: ‘He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all.’ That is, the Father gave up the Son.” What then? Did he undergo a forced handing-over? Did he suffer against his will? Who is so impious, who has so little share in the divine words and is such a stranger to the apostolic teaching, that he would dare to say that the Lord’s passion was forced, and did not come about by the will of the one who suffered? Was he handed over under compulsion who says, “I am the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep”? Is he under compulsion who says, “No one takes my life from me; I have authority to take it up again”? Did he endure the passion under compulsion who says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”? Did he endure it under compulsion who said, “I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world”? Since you bring forward a saying of Paul, which you read badly when you call the Son subordinate, listen to Paul when he says, “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself.” He emptied himself! And since it is written of the Savior that the Father gave him up for you, let us see whether we find Christ giving himself up. Paul says, “Be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma.” Do you see that his will was not forced, but in full accord with the Father? For what the Son wills, the Father also wills. And he does not lie who says, “He who has seen me has seen the Father.”

In the previous sermon it was discussed how the unequal could supposedly be revealed through the unequal. On their view, the one who has seen him who can do nothing of himself has seen him who can do all things. The one who has seen the one under authority has seen the one who has authority in his own right. The one who has seen the offspring has seen the one who begot him. The one who has seen what is created, as the heretics say, has seen the uncreated. “Yes,” one of them says, “just as works reveal the craftsmen.” For this is how the heretics take “He who has seen me has seen the Father.” “Since he is the product of the Father’s activity,” they say, “then just as great works reveal their craftsmen even when the craftsmen are not seen (a finely carved column, for example, becomes an image and likeness of the craft), so too, since he was a great work of the Father’s power, he reveals the one who made him.” What then? Would you have heaven say too, “He who has seen me, heaven, has seen God”? After all, heaven is also the product of the Creator. Then let creation seize the Son’s words for itself; let him no longer be the only one to say, “He who has seen me has seen the Father.” Let heaven say, “He who has seen me has seen God, for I too am his product.” Let the earth say as well, “He who has seen me has seen God, for he created me too.” Let the sea say as well, “He who has seen me has seen the one who [?] me, or the one who set my bounds.” Whoever knew the stars saw the one who adorned them. Who is so wretched as to share out the Master’s words among the creation?

But let what we promised run on to its fulfillment. For I want us to come prepared for the account of Noah and the whole contemplation of him, if God helps us to set it forth according to his present will. We say this not merely to open up our minds, but so that we do not miss the meanings through ignorance of the plain sense of the story. For our aim is to show that the flood, though it has the look of severity, has the force of loving-kindness, and that the whole subject of it is full of heavenly and earthly insights, drawn not from what reasoning suggests but from what Scripture itself establishes. May the God of the saints, who has granted us this evening table, grant us also the morning one, and all the days of our life, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and might for ever and ever. Amen.
